extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers of humour theory, philosophy, literary and cultural studies
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and evaluation of eighteenth- and nineteenth-century incongruity-based theories of humour and ridicule, focusing on cognitive, social, aesthetic and moral criteria for what provokes laughter and what kinds of ridicule are acceptable or effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity as cause of laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter is produced by the perception of an incongruity — a sudden perception of mismatch between ideas/concepts and real objects or between disparate ideas (Locke, Schopenhauer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the cognitive, psychological theme: the individual perceives an incongruity and responds. Examples (Schopenhauer: tangent to a circle / line appearing angled) illustrate the principle. Note caveats: cognitive accounts often ignore social context and can be challenged on moral or cultural grounds (see later examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter as socially shared and contagious
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter is not only an individual cognitive reaction but 'very contagious' and something to be socially shared; its effects and purposes must be considered in social terms (Hutcheson).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorists should account for how laughter functions within conversation and groups (e.g., clubs, coffee-houses) and how social contagion shapes its expression and consequences. Failure to consider sociality risks an incomplete account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ridicule's disciplinary and social function
rubrics_metrics.description: Ridicule serves a disciplinary role: it promotes social congruity, maintains morality, taste and good manners, and deters small vices by making potential offenders 'think twice' (Shaftesbury, Stewart, Smith, Hutcheson).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate ridicule by its social utility — e.g., its effectiveness in correcting 'smaller vices' and curbing 'extravagance, folly, and impertinence'. Recognize limits: serious moral wrongs may require indignation rather than ridicule; complete villains or wholly honest persons are not proper targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: True vs false raillery (true vs false wit)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a distinction between 'true' raillery (which serves the good sense and is tasteful) and 'false' raillery (crude or offensive); true raillery is associated with gentlemanly conduct and good breeding (Shaftesbury, Campbell).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction is often rhetorical and class-laden: what counts as 'true' is frequently asserted by those within a social circle. Theorists should note that precise criteria are hard to define and that claims of 'true' raillery can be used to exclude or dismiss other forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class/aesthetic markers of acceptable ridicule
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceptable or refined ridicule is tied to ideals of gentlemanly conversation, classical harmony, and taste; banter/raillery were socially coded (Campbell: banter coarse, raillery finer; Shaftesbury: reserved for 'gentlemen and friends').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess humour with attention to social context and status distinctions: who is producing the ridicule, where, and among whom. Beware that such markers can obscure power relations and legitimate only certain groups' humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic criterion: congruity, proportion and beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: The aesthetic standard privileged harmony and proportion; congruity is perceived as beautiful while incongruity is equated with deformity and ridiculousness (Shaftesbury, Hogarth, Lord Kames).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humour that appeals to perceived disharmony or deformation (angular lines, disproportion) is what provokes ridicule under this standard. Theorists invoking aesthetic criteria treat ridicule as responding to objectively discernible disharmony, but must justify claims of objectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper objects of ridicule (smaller improprieties)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ridicule is properly directed at 'smaller improprieties in character and manners' rather than grave moral depravity; it corrects trifling faults more effectively than grave admonition (Stewart, Hutcheson).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating targets of humour, prefer those whose faults are minor and corrective. Recognize exceptions: some objects (complete villains, utterly virtuous figures) are inappropriate targets, and misdirected ridicule can be unjust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim that the 'sense of ridicule' judges rightly
rubrics_metrics.description: Some eighteenth-century writers (Shaftesbury, Akenside, Hutcheson) argued that the faculty of ridicule is divinely or naturally bestowed and will 'only ridicule that which is actually ridiculous' — i.e., it is an objective judge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This claim can be treated as a normative standard used to justify ridicule's use. Modern readers should interrogate its presupposition of objective taste and examine empirical and ethical counterexamples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical use and abuse of ridicule (Brown's critique)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ridicule can be a rhetorical device used to 'befriend either truth or falsehood'; different social groups and disputants can use mockery to advance competing positions (John Brown's critique).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate humourers' intentions and rhetorical contexts. Beware of assuming that ridicule reliably tracks truth; assess whether mockery is being used manipulatively or to silence dissenting voices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral limits and ethical caution in examples
rubrics_metrics.description: The choice of examples in humour theory reveals moral taste and can expose ethical failures (e.g., Schopenhauer's racist example of a grieving black father is shown as morally blind and inappropriate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorists must scrutinize examples for insensitivity, exclusion, or prejudice. A sound theory of humour should avoid endorsing mockery of vulnerable people, grief, or characteristics that reflect social injustice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for context-sensitivity and cultural relativism
rubrics_metrics.description: What counts as ridiculous varies by social group and context; eighteenth-century gentlemanly ideals often ignored cross-cultural and class differences, whereas a more relativist sociological view sees the sensus communis as group-relative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humour accounts should incorporate cultural and social context — avoid assuming universal reactions. Comparative and sociological perspectives help explain humour's ubiquity across societies and the variability of acceptable targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between psychological and sociological approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Two thematic approaches exist: psychological (individual cognitive processing producing laughter) and sociological/aesthetic (functions, social purposes, and disciplinary roles of laughter and ridicule).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A comprehensive evaluation of humour should integrate both approaches: explain cognitive mechanisms and also address social functions, contagion, norms, and power dynamics. Relying on only one theme produces a partial theory.
